client: I've been really struggling lately with my final exams coming up next week, and I can't seem to stop this constant knot in my stomach. Every time I sit down to study, my mind just goes blank and I start thinking about how disappointed my parents will be if I don't do well. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the exams are still happening no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy weight right now — that knot in your stomach, the blank mind, and the fear of letting your parents down all at once is genuinely exhausting. You're right that the exams are still coming, but what we *can* work on is loosening the grip those anxious thoughts have on you, which might actually help you study more effectively. I'm curious — when your mind goes blank and you think about disappointing your parents, what's the specific thought that tends to hit you the hardest?

client: I think the thought that hits me hardest is something like, "If I fail these exams, it proves I'm not as smart as everyone thinks I am, and my parents will finally see that I've been faking it this whole time." It's like this voice in my head that's been waiting for a chance to say "I told you so." And honestly, just saying it out loud feels kind of embarrassing, because part of me knows it sounds extreme, but in the moment it feels completely true.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — it takes real courage to say it out loud, and you don't need to feel embarrassed at all, because what you're describing is actually incredibly common and has a name: **impostor syndrome**. That inner voice telling you you've been "faking it" is a thought, not a fact, and it's worth gently asking — what actual evidence do you have that you've genuinely *earned* the success you've had so far? What would you say to a close friend who told you they felt this way?

client: I mean, I guess if a friend said that to me, I'd tell them to look at their grades or the fact that they got this far, and that one exam doesn't erase all of that. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just doesn't stick the same way, like there's a wall between knowing something intellectually and actually feeling it. And I'm not sure giving the "impostor syndrome" a name really changes how real it feels when I'm sitting there staring at my textbook at midnight.
therapist: You've actually just identified something really important — that gap between *knowing* something and *feeling* it is at the heart of what we work on in CBT, and you're right that just labeling it doesn't magically close that gap. What we can do is practice building a bridge across it, not through one big insight, but through small, repeated moments of catching that voice and gently challenging it in real time. So when you're sitting there at midnight and the voice shows up, what does it actually say first — is it more "you're going to fail" or more "you don't deserve to be here"?

client: It's more the "you don't deserve to be here" one, I think, because it's less about the specific exam and more like this underlying feeling that I've somehow tricked everyone into thinking I belong in this program. And then the "you're going to fail" part comes after, almost like the punishment that's going to expose the first thing as true. I like the idea of building a bridge, but I'm honestly worried that in those midnight moments I won't even remember to try, because the anxiety kind of takes over and it's hard to think clearly enough to challenge anything.
therapist: What you're describing — that "punishment" thought following the "I don't belong" thought — is actually a really clear pattern, and the fact that you can see it so precisely right now is genuinely valuable. You're right that midnight anxiety makes it hard to access clear thinking, which is exactly why we'd want to build a simple "anchor phrase" *now*, something short enough that even an anxious brain can hold onto it, like "I have evidence I belong here" — almost like leaving yourself a note before the storm hits. What's one specific piece of evidence from your past that feels the most solid to you, something that even your harshest inner critic would struggle to argue with?

client: There's this one moment from last year where I got the highest grade in my class on a really difficult midterm, and my professor actually used my answer as an example for the rest of the students. I keep trying to hold onto that, but my inner critic immediately says something like "that was just one time, or maybe the bar was low, or you got lucky." I guess that's the most solid thing I have, but I'm skeptical that an anchor phrase is going to hold up against that kind of relentless counter-argument my brain throws at everything.
therapist: That moment is genuinely significant — your professor didn't just grade you, they held your thinking up as a model for others, and that's not something that happens by luck or a low bar. Your inner critic is doing something really predictable here, which is called **discounting the positive**, where it works overtime to disqualify any evidence that threatens its story. What if, instead of fighting the critic head-on with a phrase, we built a small written list of moments like this one — so that at midnight, you're not relying on memory alone but actually holding something concrete in your hand?

client: That actually makes more sense to me than the anchor phrase idea, because you're right that I can't trust my memory when I'm in that state. But I'm a little worried that when I sit down to write the list, my brain will just immediately start discounting each thing as I write it, so I'll end up with a list and a counter-argument next to every single item. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to make the list feel more solid, like something I can actually believe when I read it back.
therapist: You're thinking about this really carefully, and that instinct to anticipate the critic's moves is actually something we can use *against* it — what if, next to each item on the list, you wrote not your own defense, but the **concrete external evidence**, like your professor's actual words, a grade, something someone else said, so it's not you arguing with yourself but facts that exist outside your own head? The critic is very good at attacking your interpretations, but it has a harder time dismantling things that actually happened and were witnessed by others. What do you think — are there two or three moments like the professor one where someone outside of you clearly recognized your ability in a way you could write down almost like a quote or a fact?

client: Yeah, actually, there are a couple of things that come to mind — my advisor told me at the end of last semester that I was one of the most prepared students she'd worked with, and I got a scholarship that only three people in my program received. When I think of them as external facts like that, written down almost like evidence in a file, it does feel slightly harder for my brain to just wave them away. But I'm still a little nervous about actually doing this exercise before the exams, because part of me feels like focusing on past wins might make me complacent, like maybe the anxiety is the only thing keeping me from completely falling apart.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that fear that anxiety is actually *useful*, that it's the engine keeping you going, and without it you might collapse. This is actually one of the most common and sneaky beliefs that keeps anxiety locked in place, but here's what the evidence from your own life suggests: you earned that scholarship and your advisor's praise *while* carrying this anxiety, not because of it — your preparation came from you, not from the fear. What do you think would actually happen if you felt just a little more settled going into these exams — do you genuinely think you'd stop caring, or might you actually be able to think more clearly?

client: When you put it that way, I think honestly I probably wouldn't stop caring, because caring about doing well feels like it's just part of who I am, separate from the anxiety. But it's strange, because I've had this knot in my stomach for so long that I'm not even sure I know what "more settled" would feel like — it's almost like the anxiety has become so familiar that it feels like my baseline. I guess I'm a little afraid that if I actually try this evidence list and it helps, I'll have to admit that I've been making things harder for myself this whole time, and that feels uncomfortable in its own way.
therapist: What you just said is genuinely insightful — recognizing that the anxiety has become your "baseline" is a really meaningful shift, and it makes complete sense that imagining life without it feels almost disorienting. And that fear of "I've been making things harder for myself" — I want to gently reframe that, because learning a better way forward isn't evidence that you were failing before, it's just evidence that you're growing. If a friend came to you and said "I finally found something that helped me," would you tell them they should have figured it out sooner, or would you just feel glad they found it?

client: I'd obviously just be glad they found it, I wouldn't pile on about the timing. I think I'm starting to see what you're doing with these comparisons, and it does land a little differently when I imagine saying these things to someone else versus myself. I guess I'm willing to try making that evidence list tonight, though I'm still not fully convinced it'll hold up when the anxiety peaks, but maybe that's okay for now.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what just happened — you extended yourself the same compassion you'd offer a friend, even if just for a moment, and that's not a small thing. "Maybe that's okay for now" is actually a really healthy place to land, because you don't need to be fully convinced tonight; you just need to be willing to try, and you already are. When you sit down to make that list, what feels like the right first thing to write down — your professor's example, the scholarship, or your advisor's words?

client: I think I'd start with the professor one, because it's the most specific and vivid in my memory — I can almost picture exactly where I was sitting when he said it, so it feels the most real and hardest to dismiss. But I'm realizing as I think about writing it down that I don't remember his exact words, just the general gist, and I'm worried my brain will use that as a loophole to discount it. Is it still useful if I can't quote it word for word, or does it need to be exact to actually work?
therapist: The fact that you remember *where you were sitting* when it happened is actually powerful evidence of how real and significant that moment was — our brains anchor vivid memories in physical details precisely because they mattered. You don't need his exact words, because the verifiable fact is this: your professor chose your work, in front of everyone, as the standard to aspire to, and that happened regardless of the precise phrasing. What if you wrote it down exactly as you just described it to me — "my professor used my answer as the example for the whole class" — because that's already specific, concrete, and true?
